clue.text: Examples of confidence expressed by some of the players

definitions.text: Examples of confidence expressed by some of the players

parts.words: Examples of confidence expressed by some of the players
parts.note: a confidence is a secret told quietly, and the players are actors in a theatre, who mutter asides the whole audience can hear

explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical asides meant to be heard by the audience but not by other characters are secrets voiced on stage.

clue.text: Change trains, missing one, saying nothing

indicators.note: missing says the letter for one is dropped from the word trains

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
someone saying nothing is mute

explanation.surface: A rail traveller switches trains on a journey without a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' takes I (one) out of TRAINS, leaving TRANS.
explanation.definitionFit: To transmute is to transform something, a formal synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Dirt — get to remove last of it around lip

indicators.note: this word is a container marker: it says one piece is placed inside the other, and the clue words of the pieces show which way round
to remove says a letter is taken away from the word get

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: last of picks the final letter of the word it

parts.note: a lip is the rim of a cup or bowl

explanation.surface: An instruction to scrub away dirt from the edge of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to remove' strips the final letter of 'it' from 'get'; 'around' wraps what is left about the edge word. 'lip' looks like a mouth, but is an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Grime is ingrained dirt or soot, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Argument blowing up about headgear — fellow gets reprimand

indicators.note: about says those scrambled letters go around the next pieces
blowing up suggests an explosion, so the letters of the word for argument are scattered

parts.note: an argument is a row
a hat is headgear

explanation.surface: A quarrel over a hat flares up, and one man gets told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blowing up' scrambles the quarrel word, and 'about' wraps it round the headgear and the fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone what for is an informal idiom for scolding them severely.

clue.text: Vessel rocks about, spilling uranium out

parts.note: rocks is slang for ice, as in a drink on the rocks

indicators.note: spilling suggests letters tumbling out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged
out says the letter for uranium is taken from the word about

parts.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A ship pitches about on rocks, leaking radioactive cargo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes U from ABOUT, leaving ABOT, which 'spilling' rearranges as BOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: An iceboat is a craft on runners that sails over frozen water, a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Chairman's in favour of heraldic band with gold tint

parts.note: pro means in favour of
a fess is a broad horizontal band across a heraldic shield
or is the heraldic tincture gold

explanation.surface: A company chairman backs a coat of arms with a horizontal stripe and gilt colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: In heraldry the colours are called tinctures, and the gold one is named or.
explanation.definitionFit: A university professor holds a chair, so the holder of a chair is a chairman in a punning sense.

clue.text: Greek character getting doctor to prescribe lozenge

parts.note: rho is the Greek letter R
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A Greek man gets a doctor to prescribe a throat sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lozenge' looks like a cough sweet to be prescribed, but it is the diamond shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhomb is an equal-sided parallelogram, the diamond shape also called a lozenge.

clue.text: Liberal, one extremely reticent about politician joining an institution in the City?

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
extremely means very

indicators.note: about says the word for reticent goes around the next pieces

parts.note: someone reticent is coy
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy Liberal MP is drawn into some establishment in London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' has the shy word enclose the politician and 'an'. The City is London's financial district, where these historic trade guilds are based.
explanation.definitionFit: London's livery companies are ancient trade guilds based in the City, its financial square mile.

clue.text: Exchanging vehicle in industrial area

parts.note: exchanging goods is trading
an estate is an estate car, a British name for a station wagon

explanation.surface: Someone swaps cars on a business park.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate car is the British term for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: A trading estate is a British term for a zone of factories and warehouses, an industrial park.

clue.text: Silly to go round one flat showing no signs of life

indicators.note: to go round says the word for silly encloses the next pieces

parts.note: silly means inane
one is the Roman numeral I
mat or matt describes a flat, unglossy finish

explanation.surface: A foolish lodger wanders round a flat, and it seems lifeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go round' has the silly word enclose the rest. 'flat' looks like an apartment, but it is a dull finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanimate means lifeless, without any sign of life.

clue.text: Gatecrashing our party will get you a reputation

indicators.note: something gatecrashing enters where it was not invited, so the word for party gets inside the word our

parts.note: taken as written
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Gatecrashers at our party will earn you a bad name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reputation' looks unrelated to smell, but odour has an old sense of standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Odour can mean repute or standing, as in being in good or bad odour with someone.

clue.text: Go after private facility, missing it

indicators.note: missing says the word it is dropped from the bathroom term

parts.note: an en suite is a private bathroom attached to a bedroom
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel guest leaves after finding the private bathroom out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking IT out of ENSUITE leaves ENSUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow on afterwards, a synonym of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Cultivated area ran round romantic bower

indicators.note: round says the word for ran encloses the next letters

parts.note: to run away is to flee, so ran is fled

indicators.note: romantic suggests something fanciful and freely reworked, so the letters of bower are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone runs around a lovers' arbour in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'romantic' scrambles the arbour word, and 'round' has the word for ran enclose it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed of flowers is a cultivated plot in a garden.

clue.text: Like policemen in Uruguay, taken in by that German?

indicators.note: taken in by says the letter for Uruguay goes inside the word for that

parts.note: yon is an old word for that
U was the international vehicle code for Uruguay

explanation.surface: A German wonders what police officers in Uruguay are like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' puts the country's letter inside the old word for that. The definition plays on the saying that policemen look ever more youthful as you age.
explanation.definitionFit: A familiar saying of middle age is that police officers seem to grow more youthful every year.

clue.text: Worker on strike?

parts.note: a strike here is a find of precious metal, not a walkout, and the worker is a prospector digging for it

explanation.definitionFit: A prospector who digs for the yellow metal hopes to make a strike, a rich find.

clue.text: Response to cricket cheats, means of avoiding explosive situation?

definitions.meaning: a player caught cheating can be barred from playing Test matches, the top international games of cricket
a treaty banning nuclear weapons tests keeps bombs from being detonated

explanation.surface: A cricket board's punishment for cheats is also said to defuse tension.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspension from Test matches punishes cricketers, and a treaty halting nuclear detonations is the familiar arms-control sense.

clue.text: Pulse generated by acceleration in less frequented route over Scottish mountain?

indicators.note: over in a down clue puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: a B-road is a minor British road, quieter than an A-road

indicators.note: in says the letter for acceleration goes inside the mountain word

parts.note: ben is a Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis
a is the symbol for acceleration in physics

explanation.surface: A heartbeat quickens as someone drives a quiet road over a Highland peak.
explanation.walkthrough: B-roads are Britain's secondary roads. A goes inside BEN to give BEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are edible seeds of legumes, and this large flat bean is one of them.

clue.text: New Ravel work's about to show common ground with another piece

definitions.text: show common ground with another piece

indicators.note: about says the word for work goes around the next letters

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work

indicators.note: new means the letters of Ravel are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A new recording of Ravel turns out to share ground with another composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' turns RAVEL into VERLA, and OP goes 'about' it: O(VERLA)P.
explanation.definitionFit: Things overlap when they partly cover the same area, sharing some ground.

clue.text: Prince carrying orphan's basket

indicators.note: carrying says the abbreviation for prince holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: Annie is the orphan of the comic strip and musical Little Orphan Annie

explanation.surface: A prince carries an orphan girl's basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' has the prince abbreviation hold the orphan's name, from the musical about the red-haired orphan.
explanation.definitionFit: A pannier is a basket slung over a pack animal or bicycle.

clue.text: Regulations about old car having rust

indicators.note: about says the word for regulations goes around the next pieces

parts.note: a code is a body of regulations
RR, Rolls-Royce, is a car

explanation.surface: Rules are broken over an ancient car that is falling apart with rust.
explanation.walkthrough: CODE goes 'about' RR and O: CO(RRO)DE. 'rust' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To corrode is to be eaten away chemically, as iron is when it rusts.

clue.text: Pipe replaced in a trench

indicators.note: replaced means the letters are put back in a new order

explanation.surface: A pipe is laid again in a trench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaced' rearranges A and TRENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: The chanter is the fingered pipe of a set of bagpipes, which plays the melody.

clue.text: Complaint from a union MEP represented

indicators.note: represented is read as re-presented, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: A Member of the European Parliament files a grievance on behalf of a union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' rearranges A UNION MEP. 'Complaint' looks like a grievance but is an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint can mean an illness, and pneumonia is an infection of the lungs.

clue.text: Sensation of languor in Charleroi unnerving on reflection

indicators.note: on reflection says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A visitor feels listless after an unsettling stay in the Belgian city of Charleroi.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'Charleroi unnerving' is IUNNE, which 'on reflection' turns round. 'in' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is weary listlessness or boredom, a feeling of lethargy.

clue.text: Trainee acted improperly

indicators.note: improperly says the letters are set out wrongly, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trainee behaved badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'improperly' rearranges ACTED.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young person training for the armed forces or police.

clue.text: Painter's bunk giving firm support

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece that gives support sits underneath, so the word for bunk goes below the word for firm

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
bunk is nonsense, and so is rot

explanation.surface: An artist's bed gives solid support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bunk' looks like a bed, but means nonsense. As the clue goes down, ROT is underneath CO, holding it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot was a nineteenth-century French landscape artist.

clue.text: Sample of porn in online material

indicators.note: Sample of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A taste of internet porn is offered as material.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run through 'porn in online'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninon is a lightweight sheer fabric of silk or nylon, a dress material.

clue.text: Cut off one part, retaining centre, possibly

indicators.note: retaining says the pieces for one and part keep the next letters between them

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of centre could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Someone removes one section while keeping the middle, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges the centre word, and 'retaining' has the one-and-part pieces hold it between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To intercept is to stop something in transit, cutting it off from its destination.

clue.text: Tabloid journalism's the same whichever way you look at it

definitions.text: the same whichever way you look at it

parts.note: the Mirror is a British tabloid newspaper
journalism is a form of writing

explanation.surface: A claim that tabloid reporting is identical whatever angle you take.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mirror is a British tabloid. Script written backwards reads normally once held up to a looking glass, so it is legible either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Reversed script looks correct in a looking glass, so it can be read either directly reversed or reflected.
